newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel puts brakes on East Jerusalem enclave.
newsitem.headline: Israel puts brakes on East Jerusalem enclave.

text.p: Israel on Monday suspended a permit to build a new Jewish enclave in Arab East Jerusalem, putting the brakes on a project which Palestinians say will bury the Middle East peace process.

The Interior Ministry said a ministry committee had ruled that construction on the site, in the Ras al-Amoud Arab neighbourhood on the slopes of the Mount of Olives, could not proceed until an appeal against the plan had been heard.
The Jerusalem District Appeal Committee will hold a preliminary hearing on the challenge, filed on Sunday by two left-wing members of the Jerusalem city council, on August 5, the written ruling said.
"The permit cannot be granted until a ruling is made on the appeal," ministry spokeswoman Tova Ellinson said.
The move, though technical, bought time for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to try to defuse the latest crisis in Israel's embittered relations with the Palestinian Authority.

Netanyahu vowed last week to block the project "at this time" after a surprise decision by Israel's Jerusalem municipality to allow U.S. Jewish magnate Irving Moskowitz to build 70 settler homes on land he owns in Ras al-Amoud.
Palestinians, who claim East Jerusalem as the capital of a future state, have blasted the ruling as a "declaration of war" and say construction would wreck the peace process.
Criticism of the decision has also come from leftist opponents of the government and of Jerusalem Mayor Ehud Olmert, a member of Netanyahu's right-wing Likud bloc.

"Many Jerusalem residents feel the construction at Ras al-Amoud is aimed at setting the city on fire and furthering the mayor's personal interests," Ornan Yekutieli, one of the councillors who lodged the appeal, said.
"In the final analysis Jerusalem residents will be made to pay the price," Yekutieli told Israel Radio.
The status of East Jerusalem, which Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East War, is one of the most explosive issues dividing Israelis and Palestinians.

Netanyahu's peace talks with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat have been in crisis since March when Israel broke ground on a 6,500-home settlement on an East Jerusalem hill known to Israelis as Har Homa and to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Saeb Erekat, the PLO's senior negotiator, accused Netanyahu of using the Ras al-Amoud project to appear "dovish" to the world and divert attention from the larger settlement.
"If settlement activities continue, there really would be no peace process. Any peace intiative has to include a halt to settlement activities," Erekat told Reuters.

Israeli sources said Netanyahu had received a message on Sunday from President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt, which is seeking with the United States to revive peace talks, expressing concern about the impact of the Ras al-Amoud project on peace efforts.

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, who met Arafat in Brussels last week, was expected to discuss the row at talks in Jerusalem on Monday with PLO negotiator Nabil Shaath and was to travel to Jordan on Tuesday for a meeting with King Hussein.

Netanyahu has drawn a distinction between Har Homa, which he says he will not halt, and Ras al-Amoud, arguing that the time is not right to proceed with construction of housing for Jews in the midst of a densely populated Arab district.

In a bid to ward off right-wing criticism that he has gone soft on Jerusalem, he has insisted that his stance on Ras al-Amoud does not signal any change in policy on the city, which Israelis regard as their "united, eternal" capital.
Moskowitz, a Miami-based businessman who finances Jewish settlement in occupied territories, said on Monday that efforts to block his project played into Palestinian hands.

"If this is not a good time for building a Jewish neighbourhood on Har Hazeitim (Mount of Olives), the Arabs will feel they won a victory by their threats and intimidations and they will do everything possible to stop the project at Har Homa," he told Israel Radio before news of the suspension.
